tei:bibl.tei:title: תְּפִלָּה לִסְגֻלַּת אִשִּׁים
Prayer for a practice of divine contemplation, attributed to a Rabbi Mosheh (as found in Leiden Or. 4779, et al)
tei:bibl.tei:author: Mosheh ben Yaaqov ibn Ezra
tei:bibl.tei:note: Source: Prayer of our teacher, Rabbi Masheh in Ha-Sharon Devarim Atiqim (Moritz Steinschneider, Ha-Karmel issue 44, 12 July 1867) p. 350 https://opensiddur.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/prayer-of-our-teacher-rabbi-masheh-in-ha-sharon-devarim-atiqim-moritz-steinschneider-ha-karmel-issue-44-12-july-1867-p--350.png

tei:div.tei:p: Note: This translation uses the plural pronouns They/Their/Them to refer to God as a pluralis majestatis, and to avoid the implications of God being assigned a gender. (Find Abraham Ibn Ezra’s commentary on Genesis 1:1 for a discussion of the pluralis majestatis when referring to God.) All divine referents (pronouns, epithets, names) are rendered in unicase.

This prayer for divine contemplatives, beginning with the incipit “Tefilat Lisgulat Ishim” (prayer for distinguished individuals), is attested in several manuscripts prefaced by the title, תפלת הרב רבינו משה זצ״ל (prayer of our teacher, Rabbi Mosheh, may their righteousness be remembered for a blessing). The assumption of earlier scholars was that the Rabbi Mosheh here refers to Rabbi Mosheh ben Maimon — Maimonides (1138-1204). While our reading of the prayer finds nothing outside the concepts articulated by Rambam in his Mishneh Torah (Yesodei haTorah) and Moreh Nevukhim, it seems more likely that the Rabbi Mosheh referred to here is the famous paytan Mosheh ben Yaaqov ibn Ezra (ca. 1055-after 1138), who is quoted sharing similar ideas as found in this prayer by Rabbi Abraham ben Azriel in Arugat ha-Bosem (ca. 1230).

This transcription, vocalization, and transcription was made from fol. 150a in Warner 41 (Leiden Or. 4779). Moritz Steinschneider (1815-1907), in his Catalogus codicum hebraeorum Bibliothecae academiae Lugduno Batavae ([Leiden]: E. J. Brill. 1858). p. 188, describes the manuscript and folio as follows:

The scholar Eliakim Carmoly (1802-1875) provided the reference to this or a related manuscript in his 1842 work עקטאן. Moritz Steinschneider follows Carmoly (in Aqtan [1842], p. 4) in identifying “Rabbi Mosheh” as Maimnonides. This attribution was repeated in Steinschneider’s transcription of the prayer published in the column, “Ha-Sharon: Devarim Atiqim” in Ha-Karmel (no. 44, 12 July 1867, cumulative page 350). There he introduces the text, “התפלה הזאת נעתקה לי מכ״י הנמצא באוקספורד, ושכחתי לציין ציונו ומספרו, ואין ספק שהיא היא התפלה המיוחסת לרמב״ם בכ״‬י פאריז מספר 837 (לפי הרשימה החדשה)‭ ‬המתחלת ג״כ תפלה לסגולת אישים.” (This prayer was transcribed for me from a manuscript located in Oxford, but I forgot to record its catalog mark and number. There is no doubt, however, that it is the same prayer attributed to the Rambam [=Rabbi Moses ben Maimon] found in the Paris manuscript no. 837 (according to the new catalog), which likewise begins: “A Prayer for Distinguished Individuals.”). While the location of this Oxford manuscript remains unknown, Steinschneider’s transcription is very close to our own with only a few missing words.

Alexander Suessman Muntner (1897-1973) located a similar manuscript explicitly attributed to Maimonides: “a Hebrew manuscript in the Bibliothèque Nationale de Paris which is entitled ‘The Prayer of Moses Maimonides’...Hebrew manuscript no. 873, pt. 7, fol. 98V°, described in the catalogue as follows: ‘Prayer of Rabbi Moses Maimonides, beginning with Tefila Lisegulas Eeshim and terminating by the piece of verse Galgal Soveiv‘” (Rosner, Medicine in the Bible and Talmud, p. 132, citing Bibliothèque nationale, Catalogues des manuscripts hébreux et samaritains de la Bibliothèque impériale (Paris, 1866), p. 142). Taking the attribution to Maimonides at face value, Fred Rosner (1935-2024) follows Muntner in dismissing the prayer as a forgery. Rosner considered the “astrological” imagery and style antithetical to Maimonides. What may have also given pause to scholars was the admission by Steinschneider that he had forgotten the shelf mark to the mansucript from which his transcription purportedly derived. The second manuscript Steinschneider mentioned in his published transcription, Paris Ms. Hébreu 873, had been handled by Eliakim Carmoly — a scholar whose reputation had been sullied by accusations of forgery. Meanwhile, it is unclear to me whether anyone concerned with the authenticity of the prayer text checked Warner 41, fol. 150.

It is almost too easy to forget the pleasant and beneficial conditions under which we operate today when so many page images are available online. Not only are we grateful to the archivists and librarians at the University of Leiden who made this resource accessible, but to the entire vision and funding apparatus in the Netherlands and the European Union seeking to preserve and make publicly accessible such treasures. Steinschneider’s transcription from that 1867 issue of Ha-Karmel was accessed via the National Library of Israel’s historical newspaper database and we are grateful to all those who work to maintain and grow that database. Translations of my Latin transcriptions from Steinschneider’s catalogues were aided by Google Translate and ChatGPT (OpenAI).

For this work published here at the Open Siddur, we are grateful to Simcha Daniel Burstyn and Nir Krakauer for correcting my transcription, and for proposing the current vocalization. My digital transcription used Steinschneider’s printed transcription in Ha-Karmel as a base text. Nir was able to correct this transcription after I located Warner 41 and fol. 150 in the collection of the University of Leiden. Nir also offered compelling annotation including relevant citations to Maimonides’ Mishneh Torah and Moreh Nevukhim. As far as I know, this is the first time this work has been translated in any language.

We hope to uncomplicate the history of this prayer. We welcome scholars with an expertise in 12th century Jewish neo-Aristotelian philosophy to comment on the content of the prayer and its parts and whether they may have been composed within the circle of his students dedicated to contemplative Jewish practice.

tei:note.tei:p: Rosner’s opinion on this prayer appears in a digression made in his 1967 article “The Physicians Prayer attributed to Moses Maimonides“, that largely focuses on yet another prayer attributed to Maimonides that first appears in German in 1783, and is later attributed to the student of Immanuel Kant and doctor to Moses Mendelssohn, Dr. Markus Herz.
